speaker: Petter Hörnfeldt
title: Ep16 - Interview with Petter Hoernfeldt - Mentour Pilot
question: In commercial aviation, how does teaching as a simulator instructor transform a pilot's own operational capability?
guest: I didn't feel at 23 that I was fully ready to be a good captain. I could have been a common captain, but I wanted to be a good captain. So I applied to the synthetic flight instructor role, which first officers are invited to apply for in my airline. That was transformational. I recommend it to anyone who wants to hone their skills and understanding, because it's one thing doing the craft—flying the aircraft—but a completely different thing to know it at a level where you can explain it so someone else understands it. During my SFI training and first year, I saw so many different ways of flying the aircraft, good ways and less good ways, and I was taught how to speak up to people well above my pay grade. I realized pretty quickly that the only way to do that is to really know your stuff. People will listen if you can motivate why you give them feedback, but if you can't, people—especially more senior than you—will not listen, and the same goes for the cockpit.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Teaching in the simulator tends to deepen a pilot's own capability mainly by forcing them to move from knowing how to do something to understanding why it works. To explain procedures, systems and failure logic to others, instructors must master them at a level that line flying rarely demands, so their technical knowledge becomes more precise and durable.

They also gain an unusual breadth of vicarious experience. A line pilot might see a handful of serious abnormals in a career; an instructor watches hundreds of crews handle engine failures, fires, upsets and compound malfunctions, seeing the full range of errors, recoveries and decision paths. This builds a rich mental library of how situations unfold and where crews typically go wrong, which sharpens their own anticipation, threat-and-error management and decision-making.

Observing from the back seat also develops skills in monitoring, workload assessment, communication and CRM, since diagnosing others' performance and debriefing it makes instructors more self-aware and self-critical.

One caveat: manual handling skills can erode if instructing displaces actual flying, which is why operators usually require instructors to maintain line currency.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Teaching from the simulator instructor station shifts a commercial pilot from executing procedures to diagnosing how flight crews think, communicate, and fail under pressure. Explaining systems architecture, aerodynamic margins, and standard operating procedures to trainees replaces rote habit with first-principles mastery, making aircraft behavior far more predictable during complex malfunctions. Equally transformative is the vantage point behind the seats: watching dozens of crews navigate identical emergencies reveals the subtle precursors to operational breakdowns—confirmation bias, automation surprise, task saturation, and steep authority gradients—long before aircraft state becomes unstable. Under modern Evidence-Based Training frameworks, instructors constantly evaluate core competencies such as workload management, situational awareness, and decision-making, which naturally rewires their own metacognition on the line. They become quicker to recognize personal startle responses, more deliberate in briefing threats, and more receptive to input from fellow crewmembers. Finally, repeated exposure to cascading non-normal scenarios desensitizes instructors to acute stress, freeing spare mental capacity so they manage real-world disruptions with calm, structured authority.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Teaching in the simulator usually makes a pilot sharper, because instructing works as structured over-learning. To explain a procedure, a system or a failure mode, you have to understand why it works, not just how to fly it. That deepens your systems knowledge and your recall of non-normal checklists. Instructors also see far more failures than line pilots do, such as engine fires, rejected takeoffs, windshear, unreliable airspeed and dual hydraulic loss. Seeing them over and over, from the outside, builds pattern recognition and mental models that line flying rarely gives anyone.

Watching from the instructor station also trains your monitoring and threat-and-error-management skills. You learn to spot subtle crew resource management breakdowns, task saturation, confirmation bias and poor automation management in other crews. Then you start noticing the same tendencies in yourself. Debriefing builds self-critique and clear communication, which carry over into better briefings and leadership as a captain.

There are caveats. Simulators don't fully reproduce real-world pressure, fatigue or line variability. Instructors who fly very little line can lose hands-on currency and develop "sim habits," so regulators require recency and line checks. Overall, teaching tends to make a pilot more analytical and more resilient, as long as they keep flying real aircraft.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Teaching as a simulator instructor profoundly reshapes a commercial pilot’s operational capability by shifting them from simply executing procedures to understanding the deeper mechanics of flight deck performance. Explaining aircraft systems, limitations, and standard operating procedures to others forces an instructor to eliminate personal knowledge gaps and master the rationale behind every checklist and maneuver. Just as importantly, observing dozens of crews navigate abnormal and emergency scenarios from the instructor operating station accelerates pattern recognition in a way line flying rarely can. Instructors witness a wide spectrum of human-factors breakdowns—such as mode confusion, task saturation, confirmation bias, and subtle energy-state deviations—long before they might encounter them personally. When these pilots return to the line, that exposure translates into sharper threat-and-error management and earlier anticipation of developing problems. Facilitating structured debriefings also strengthens their own crew resource management, making them calmer leaders, clearer communicators, and more disciplined monitors who can recognize and correct emerging errors in themselves and their flight-deck partners.

models.answer:
Teaching in a simulator can make a commercial pilot better at spotting and correcting a developing problem before it becomes an emergency. To explain why a procedure works, the instructor has to understand the aircraft systems and the reasoning behind each step. Watching different crews handle the same failure shows how early cues get missed, how quickly workload builds, and which actions give the crew time to recover.

That experience carries over to line flying. An instructor can become quicker to notice when the aircraft or crew is falling behind, more deliberate about when to intervene, and clearer about dividing tasks and communicating under pressure. Debriefing also sharpens self-assessment. After helping others reconstruct what they saw, assumed, and decided, a pilot is better equipped to examine those same habits in their own flying.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Teaching in a simulator makes a pilot examine decisions that experience has made almost automatic. To coach a crew, the instructor has to explain which cues matter, why a procedure fits the situation, and when to change course. Watching different crews handle the same failure also shows how a small omission can grow under workload and which interventions help a crew recover.

Back in the cockpit, that practice can help the pilot recognize trouble earlier, question an initial diagnosis, and explain a decision clearly enough for the other pilot to cross-check it. It also sharpens the pilot’s sense of when to let a colleague work through a problem and when to intervene. The main gain is in judgment, monitoring, and crew coordination. Hands-on flying proficiency still depends on regular practice at the controls.
